doc.title: Wayne Andre interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 7, 2002

chapter: Writing, his own band and listening
title: Tony Bennett at Carnegie Hall and the North Texas concert
summary: He recounts getting a solo at Carnegie Hall, the mics turned off, and his own concert program after North Texas.

story.theme_name: Still working: current gigs, upcoming projects and plans

blocks.x: I did a concert, I’ll never forget this, I did a concert and I had a big solo in the concert. I did a concert with Tony Bennett at Carnegie Hall. And on the first half of the concert was Robert Farnum and we were doing the music from “Porgy & Bess.” And I just have to tell you the story how I ended up getting this solo because Buddy Morrow was actually the first trombone player but this thing, Buddy came across it and Buddy is a wonderful, wonderful cat but this thing for some reason came across written in the alto clef or some damn thing like that. And it was a spooky solo because the whole band stopped and you go, now listen carefully, [scats] you modulate right at the top [scats]. And it modulates right away and it was something that’s beautiful but you kind of had to either hear it or read it. So Buddy says, “Man, why don’t you play this thing?” So that’s how I ended up getting the solo you know. And after the rehearsal I saw all these microphones, Robert Farnum, I didn’t know Robert Farnum at all. I says, “You know this is Carnegie Hall. This music is so beautifully orchestrated. All these microphones are going to ruin the music.” He said, “Oh no, we don’t need any microphones, what are you talking about, microphones?” So because of me, all the microphones, I don’t know if they were taken down but they were shut off. And that concert was a big success concert. I’m not saying I was the reason it was a big success but I’m just saying that I hate music that sounds like over — anyways the North Texas Band, I said I don’t want any micro — we’ll have one microphone solo for a trumpet solo or just maybe two or three solo mics and that’s all we need. And my music that I write and that I played on that concert by and large — I have to be careful I don’t give myself too many accolades, but most of it, each piece is different. Each piece is different and the first piece doesn’t sound like the fourth piece. Like I did this real production number and it came out really terrific, “My Man’s Gone Now” and this was kind of maybe the highlight of the concert. And then we ended up doing the thing I wrote for Doc Severinsen which actually Bill Watrous recorded with Danny Styles, that piece “Ayo,” that kind of ended the concert. But the thing is, I haven’t © Fillius Jazz Archive -18-
heard a lot of college bands. But that night with the North Texas band, and it’s a great band, it’s always fifth gear. The energy.
It’s like getting beat on the head.
It’s just like give me a break. And it’s good, but the energy level is constant. It’s not—
So probably when your group came on it was like everybody’s ears were able to relax and really listen.
And plus it was more acoustic sounding because the microphones were taken away. And I think that had a lot to do with the article that Bill Spilka wrote in the ITA Journal.
